targets.title: Task design and second language performance: The effect of narrative type on learner output.

targets.outcome_quote:
This paper reports a replication of part of Tavakoli and Foster’s (2008) investigation into the
influence of narrative task design on second language (L2) oral performance. The initial
study found in part that narratives with both foreground and background information
elicited significantly greater syntactic complexity than those with only foreground information. This close replication adds the variable of literacy, conducting the study with adult
refugees to New Zealand with low first language (L1) literacy. Participants narrated two of
the four cartoon strips in Tavakoli and Foster (2008). In contrast to the initial study,
background information in the narrative tasks had no impact on the syntactic complexity,
lexical diversity, or fluency of performances.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The central syntactic-complexity effect explicitly contrasts with the original and the tested hypotheses are not upheld. The null lexical-diversity comparison for these two tasks is consistent across studies, but the authors do not frame that as partial support for their target finding; failure concerns the designed test of background-event effects. Explanations involving visual literacy do not declare the attempt incapable of adjudicating.

reasoning: Verified full title and all five authors. New adult refugee sample re-tests Tavakoli and Foster (2008). Ryan et al. (2023) and Foster and Skehan (1996) describe a separate prior project, not targets re-tested here.
